raw_case_text:
The patient is a 67-year-old male with a medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and sleep apnea, with no family history of neuromuscular disorders. The patient gave written and oral consent for the images and this report. 
He arrived at the hospital with complaints of bilateral ptosis, bilateral facial weakness, and bulbar symptoms, including dysarthria and difficulty with mastication. He reported having slurred speech and trouble with chewing, especially from his right side, as well as droopy eyelids on both sides 48 hours before coming to the hospital, and facial drooping, more prominent on the right side, 24 hours before coming to the hospital. His coworkers noticed the facial droop and urged the patient to seek urgent medical attention. At the emergency department, the patient arrived stable, breathing on room air without any respiratory distress. Upon further questioning, the patient reported feeling easily fatigued for the past month. He denied experiencing double vision, respiratory distress, weakness, sensory symptoms, or difficulty walking, and there have been no recent changes in medication or travel history. In terms of his social history, the patient is a man who has sex with other men. His last sexual encounter was four months before admission.
Upon examination, the patient was fully oriented but had moderate dysarthria and no aphasia. His gaze was midline, with more pronounced ptosis in the right eye than the left. Ptosis was slightly fatigable with upgaze without causing double vision. The patient exhibited bilateral facial weakness, which was more pronounced on the right side, in a lower motor pattern. According to the Medical Research Council, muscle strength was graded 5/5 in both the upper and lower extremities. The sensation of pinprick, vibration, and proprioception was normal. Reflexes were +1 throughout. The patient had an erythematous rash on both legs. Head and neck computed tomography angiography (CTA), as well as brain MRI with and without contrast, were unremarkable. Figure 1a and 1b show the patient's rash and his MRI findings.
The patient's initial labs revealed increased inflammatory markers and positive rapid plasma reagin (RPR), which, in conjunction with the rash, were indicative of syphilis. In light of the bulbar symptoms, a myasthenia panel and a lumbar puncture were ordered. Table 1 shows laboratory results and CSF analysis. 
Given the positive VDRL on CSF, elevated CSF protein, and lymphocytic pleocytosis, the patient was diagnosed with neurosyphilis; his neurological symptoms were attributed to early symptomatic neurosyphilis. He was treated with intravenous penicillin G for one week and was later switched to intravenous ceftriaxone. The patients' facial weakness, ptosis, and difficulty swallowing improved rapidly. 
One week after discharge, the myasthenia/Eaton-Lambert panel returned: acetylcholine receptor binding antibody was positive at 0.33 nmol/L; P/Q and MuSK antibodies were undetectable. Neurology contacted the patient and arranged follow-up; at that time, he reported no further symptoms. Two to three days after discharge, he was seen in the clinic and had a normal examination without ptosis, facial weakness, or proximal weakness.
Four months after symptom onset, the patient underwent electrodiagnostic testing while asymptomatic. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated normal sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) and compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs)with no evidence of axonal or demyelinating damage. Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) (3 Hz) of the right ulnar, spinal accessory, and facial nerves showed no decremental response. SFEMG was performed on the frontalis, which demonstrated increased jitter without blocking: the overall mean consecutive difference (MCD) was 72.6 mus, and five of 21 fiber pairs had MCDs greater than 74.1 mus (laboratory normal for frontalis approximately <35-40 mus). No blocking was observed. These SFEMG findings, together with a positive acetylcholine receptor binding antibody, supported the diagnosis of MG (see Appendices).
At this point, in retrospect, it was concluded that the patient's initial symptoms were unlikely to be related to neurosyphilis. The patient most likely had early asymptomatic neurosyphilis simultaneously with MG. One year after the onset of symptoms, the patient remains asymptomatic. His last RPR qualitative study was non-reactive.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 67-year-old man presented with a 48-hour history of bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, and difficulty chewing, followed by a 24-hour history of right-predominant bilateral facial weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One month prior to admission, the patient noticed easy fatigability. Forty-eight hours before presentation, he developed bilateral droopy eyelids (worse on the right), slurred speech, and difficulty chewing on the right side, followed 24 hours later by right-predominant facial drooping noticed by his coworkers.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and obstructive sleep apnea; negative family history for neuromuscular disorders. Identifies as a man who has sex with men (MSM), with his last sexual encounter 4 months prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1-month fatigability, bilateral ptosis, facial weakness, dysarthria, dysphagia/mastication difficulty, and bilateral leg rash; negative for diplopia, dyspnea, limb weakness, sensory changes, gait difficulty, recent medication changes, or travel.

objective.physical_examination: The patient was alert, fully oriented, and eupneic on room air. Cranial nerve examination revealed moderate dysarthria without aphasia, midline ocular gaze without diplopia, right-greater-than-left bilateral ptosis that was mildly fatigable on sustained upgaze, and right-predominant bilateral lower-motor-neuron-pattern facial weakness. Motor strength was 5/5 throughout all extremities, sensory exam (pinprick, vibration, proprioception) was intact, and deep tendon reflexes were 1+ symmetrically. Cutaneous examination revealed an erythematous rash on both lower extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial blood tests demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers.
objective.advanced_workup: Head and neck CT angiography and brain MRI with and without contrast were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated CSF protein. Serum myasthenia gravis panel returned 1 week post-discharge with positive acetylcholine receptor (AChR) binding antibody at 0.33 nmol/L (negative anti-MuSK and P/Q-type VGCC antibodies). Outpatient electrodiagnostic studies at 4 months showed normal nerve conduction studies and 3-Hz repetitive nerve stimulation, but abnormal frontalis single-fiber EMG (SFEMG) with increased jitter (mean consecutive difference 72.6 us; 5/21 fiber pairs >74.1 us, normal <35-40 us) confirming ocular/bulbar myasthenia gravis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed concurrent early neurosyphilis / secondary syphilis (leg rash, positive serum RPR, and positive CSF VDRL with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein) and acetylcholine-receptor-positive generalized/bulbar myasthenia gravis (AChR antibody 0.33 nmol/L and abnormal frontalis SFEMG). Treated with intravenous penicillin G for 1 week followed by intravenous ceftriaxone, with rapid complete resolution of ptosis, facial weakness, and bulbar symptoms within days of discharge; at 1-year follow-up, he remained asymptomatic with a non-reactive serum RPR.
